To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the performance metrics are useful in quantitatively evaluating the performance of visual servo methods, (ii) the performance of a method depends heavily upon the task, and (iii) the partitioned methods perform significantly better than the IBVS method for the canonical tasks considered in this paper.

(1) traditional IBVS is a robust method for simple tasks, but fails for more complex tasks, (2) partitioned IBVS methods are more robust than traditional IBVS for all tasks, (3) the choice of partitioned approach depends on the specific task, and (4) all methods fail under non-ideal conditions.

(1) partitioning of the visual servo control law can improve performance in some situations; (2) partitioning can degrade performance in other situations; and (3) the choice of partitioning method depends upon the task being performed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of visual servoing algorithms for specific tasks and experimental conditions.
the following issues: 1) How does one evaluate the performance of an image based visual servo controller?
evaluating the relative strengths of several visual servo methods for specific tasks, under specific experimental conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the partitioned methods outperform the traditional IBVS method.
the traditional IBVS method is the most robust of all the methods considered.
there is no single method which outperforms all others for all four tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the partitioned approaches perform better than IBVS in most situations, and that the choice of a specific partitioned approach is highly dependent on the task to be performed.
partitioned methods perform well in tasks for which they were developed, but that the traditional IBVS method performs well in tasks for the which the partitioned methods were not designed.
, for the tasks and experimental conditions we have considered, the traditional IBVS method performs well for simple motions, and the partitioned methods perform well when the task is difficult.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of visual servo method is task specific.
there is no one-size fits-all solution to the visual servo problem.
no single approach is optimal for all visual servoing tasks.
